title: Announcing novyn-looped-decider-0.9 | Novyn Labs
excerpt: An open-weight, state-of-the-art looped decision model. How we built and evaluated it, and why we are building it at Novyn.
content_text: Today we are announcing novyn-looped-decider-0.9, an open-weight, state-of-the-art looped decision model. Given an input and a list of options, it picks one. novyn-looped-decider-0.9 is built on Thinking Machines Lab’s newly-released TML-d24-varloop-research model, with the number of loops set to ten and a decision head trained on top of the frozen base. It chooses among up to 255 options directly, without generating text or a reasoning trace. In this post, we explain how we built and evaluated the model and share why we are building it at Novyn. What is a looped decision model? A decision model is a classifier that takes its task from the prompt. It receives an input together with a set of possible answers and returns its choice directly, which suits tasks such as routing and labeling that do not need free-form text. A looped model applies part of its network more than once. In TML-d24-varloop-research, the middle layers share a single set of weights and the number of passes through them is chosen at inference time, so each additional pass gives the model more computation on the same input without adding parameters. A looped decision model is a decision model built on a looped base. It can spend more computation on each input and still answer with a single choice instead of generated text. How it is built We start from TML-d24-varloop-research, the variable-loop counterpart to Inkling 2 Mini, which Thinking Machines Lab released with open weights on 20 November. It is a 24-layer transformer whose middle 12 layers are looped, and we run those layers ten times for every request. The base model stays frozen. On top of it we train a single decision head, a 255 × 2,304 matrix that maps the model’s hidden state to one score per option, and the highest-scoring option is returned as the answer. Evaluation We evaluated novyn-looped-decider-0.9 on the public text cases of JevBench. In a fresh run of the full model, it answered 210 of 231 cases correctly, an accuracy of 90.91%, improving on the copied native head, which answers 209. Public JevBench accuracy novyn-looped-decider-0.990.91% 210/231 Jev 1.1490.48% 209/231 Perplexity Decider 1.390.04% 208/231 GPT-6 Luna Decisions89.61% 207/231 Liquid d1.288.74% 205/231 Jev 1.1386.58% 200/231 Reference models were run with their native question types and novyn-looped-decider-0.9 with finite-choice prompts. No JevBench examples were used for training. Speed We measured serving speed with the model running ten passes on four NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Across 1,000 requests, novyn-looped-decider-0.9 returned a decision in a median of 62.8 milliseconds, and 95% of requests completed within 238.6 milliseconds. 62.8 msmedian 238.6 ms95th percentile 1,000/1,000successful requests The test repeated the 231 JevBench prompts, which range from 204 to 4,369 tokens, one request at a time. The prompt cache was cleared before each request and 20 warmup requests were excluded, so no request benefited from a cached prompt. Timing covers input processing, local HTTP, the model call and the final choice. It excludes startup, cache clearing and internet delay. This is a warm, serial serving test, not a test under concurrent load. Why we are building it Novyn is the autonomous model factory for companies. We find, train and serve the models employees need, and the first step is finding which tasks are worth a model. To do that, we categorize the tasks employees do. Agent activity and computer-use traces show work as it happens, and we are building novyn-looped-decider-0.9 to be the shared task classifier that assigns each task to a category, so the same kind of work is grouped together across different people. Tasks from many employees, grouped by Novyn Three employees produce agent tasks and computer-use traces. Their task cards travel along three lanes that join into one line and pass through a loop, which stands for novyn-looped-decider-0.9. At the top of the loop each card takes the colour of its task category. The line then splits into three, and each card lights up its slot in the matching bucket: invoices, support or research. Every bucket ends up holding tasks from employees A, B and C. This is an illustration. A B C employees agent tasks + computer traces shared task buckets A B C novyn-looped-decider-0.9 one shared task classifier invoices support research Illustration. Letters track employees A, B and C. A task takes the color of its category at the top of the loop. With tasks grouped this way, we can see which ones repeat often enough to deserve a specialist model. What’s next We are already training the next model, and we will continue to train models in this lineage. We will also publish a full technical write-up covering the model, training data, evaluation and serving setup. content_html_zh:
Today we are announcing novyn-looped-decider-0.9, an open-weight, state-of-the-art looped decision model. Given an input and a list of options, it picks one.

novyn-looped-decider-0.9 is built on Thinking Machines Lab’s newly-released TML-d24-varloop-research model, with the number of loops set to ten and a decision head trained on top of the frozen base. It chooses among up to 255 options directly, without generating text or a reasoning trace.

In this post, we explain how we built and evaluated the model and share why we are building it at Novyn.

What is a looped decision model?

A decision model is a classifier that takes its task from the prompt. It receives an input together with a set of possible answers and returns its choice directly, which suits tasks such as routing and labeling that do not need free-form text.

A looped model applies part of its network more than once. In TML-d24-varloop-research, the middle layers share a single set of weights and the number of passes through them is chosen at inference time, so each additional pass gives the model more computation on the same input without adding parameters.

A looped decision model is a decision model built on a looped base. It can spend more computation on each input and still answer with a single choice instead of generated text.

How it is built

We start from TML-d24-varloop-research, the variable-loop counterpart to Inkling 2 Mini, which Thinking Machines Lab released with open weights on 20 November. It is a 24-layer transformer whose middle 12 layers are looped, and we run those layers ten times for every request.

The base model stays frozen. On top of it we train a single decision head, a 255 × 2,304 matrix that maps the model’s hidden state to one score per option, and the highest-scoring option is returned as the answer.

评估

We evaluated novyn-looped-decider-0.9 on the public text cases of JevBench. In a fresh run of the full model, it answered 210 of 231 cases correctly, an accuracy of 90.91%, improving on the copied native head, which answers 209.

Reference models were run with their native question types and novyn-looped-decider-0.9 with finite-choice prompts. No JevBench examples were used for training.

Speed

We measured serving speed with the model running ten passes on four NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Across 1,000 requests, novyn-looped-decider-0.9 returned a decision in a median of 62.8 milliseconds, and 95% of requests completed within 238.6 milliseconds.

62.8 msmedian

238.6 ms95th percentile

1,000/1,000successful requests

The test repeated the 231 JevBench prompts, which range from 204 to 4,369 tokens, one request at a time. The prompt cache was cleared before each request and 20 warmup requests were excluded, so no request benefited from a cached prompt.

Timing covers input processing, local HTTP, the model call and the final choice. It excludes startup, cache clearing and internet delay. This is a warm, serial serving test, not a test under concurrent load.

Why we are building it

Novyn is the autonomous model factory for companies. We find, train and serve the models employees need, and the first step is finding which tasks are worth a model.

To do that, we categorize the tasks employees do. Agent activity and computer-use traces show work as it happens, and we are building novyn-looped-decider-0.9 to be the shared task classifier that assigns each task to a category, so the same kind of work is grouped together across different people.

With tasks grouped this way, we can see which ones repeat often enough to deserve a specialist model.

We are already training the next model, and we will continue to train models in this lineage. We will also publish a full technical write-up covering the model, training data, evaluation and serving setup.
